claims.text: RHEAs exhibit superior thermoelastic recovery at high temperatures relative to conventional refractory alloys.
RHEAs exhibit superior mechanical resistance at high temperatures relative to conventional refractory alloys.
High configurational entropy produces significant lattice distortion in RHEAs.
High configurational entropy produces short-range ordering in RHEAs.
The proposed RHEA has a single-phase microstructure after casting and homogenization.
The proposed RHEA contains pronounced lattice distortion and signs of short-range ordering.
The RHEA and a conventional or low-entropy refractory alloy will undergo identical high-temperature loading and heat-treatment cycles.
Above 1000°C, under the proposed controlled strain-rate conditions, dislocation creep and thermoelastic effects are the dominant deformation processes.
Lattice distortion creates local energy barriers and pinning sites for dislocations.
Short-range ordering provides additional resistance to dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion and short-range ordering jointly stabilize the dislocation structure during cyclic or sustained loading.
Stabilization of the dislocation structure enhances thermoelastic recovery.
The RHEA will have a lower high-temperature creep rate than the baseline alloy.
The RHEA will have a higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The RHEA will exhibit greater thermoelastic recovery than the baseline alloy.
In situ TEM will reveal dislocation dynamics distinct from those in the baseline and attributable to lattice distortion and short-range ordering.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the microstructure retains its lattice distortion and short-range ordering during high-temperature testing.
Phase transformations may influence the observed high-temperature mechanical behavior.
